dct_description_sm: The consequences of prenatal exposure to environmental contaminants (EC) have become a key public policy issue. This is due to evidence from several studies of intellectual impairments, learning disabilities and illness attributable to in utero exposure to EC, and to the particular vulnerability of the developing child. Knowledge improvement in this domain requires the design and implementation of prospective, longitudinal cohorts of pregnant women and children with exposure assessments at critical windows and sensitive endpoints documented along the continuum of human development. Among the several studies of effects of EC conducted so far, follow-ups through adolescence are scarce. Because fish and marine mammals represent an important part of the diet of the Inuit, exposure to mercury (Hg), polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) and chlorinated pesticides are of particular concern for public health authorities in circumpolar countries. PCBs and chlorinated pesticides have endocrine disruptive properties. They are carried from industrialized countries to the Arctic by long-range atmospheric transport, waterways, and oceanic currents. Hg contamination is rising in the North due to increasing emissions in developing countries and long range transport of Hg emissions to the North, challenging the health of the Inuit population. Elevated levels of PCBs and Hg in Northern Quebec (Nunavik) Inuit newborns and mothers of childbearing age were reported by our group. Most PCB and Hg cohort studies conducted to date have focused on growth and cognitive outcomes, with emotional and behavioral effects documented in few PCB studies but those effects have not been looked at in Hg cohort studies.
